To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the prevalence of obesity in women has increased in the past 20 years, and the increase has been most dramatic in women who are middle-aged or older, (2) the prevalence of overweight in young women has increased in recent decades, (3) the prevalence of underweight has decreased in young women, and (4) overweight and obesity are associated with an increased risk of chronic diseases.
The study of obesity in women is important because of the health risks associated with obesity.
the relationship between overweight and socioeconomic status (SES) is bidirectional.

a broad range of issues in the sociology of health, medicine and the body, including: the sociology of health and illness, medical sociology, the sociology of the body, gender and health, the sociology of ageing, and the social aspects of disability.

it is possible to use the data from a national survey of women's health to examine a variety of factors related to overweight and obesity.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the relationship between socioeconomic status and body mass index (BMI) is complex.
the association between BMI and SES varies by race/ethnicity, and that SES may influence BMI differently in men and women.
